screens.title: Managing Processes and Services
screens.narratorSegment: Today we will build a clear mental model of processes and services on RHEL and learn the essential commands you will use every day. A process is a running instance of a program, and a service is a background process that systemd manages continuously. You will see how to inspect active programs with tools like ps, top, and htop; how to send signals to stop misbehaving processes with kill; and how to control systemd services with systemctl start, stop, restart, reload, enable and disable. We will also cover how to read service logs with journalctl for effective troubleshooting. These skills matter because they let you keep services available, diagnose resource issues, and avoid data loss by choosing the right action. For example, you will learn when to request a graceful shutdown versus when a forced kill is appropriate. By the end of this lesson you will be able to list processes, identify PIDs, safely stop a runaway program, and manage service startup behavior so your system boots into the correct state. As you watch, think about which commands you would use to investigate a slow server and which to use only as a last resort.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on four practical skills that form the foundation of process and service management on RHEL. First, you will learn to identify and understand system processes using viewing tools. This means reading columns like PID, USER, C P U and memory and recognizing what a runaway process looks like. Second, you will practice controlling processes by sending signals with safe defaults first, then escalations only when necessary. That skill keeps systems stable without risking corruption. Third, you will manage services using systemd through the systemctl commands to start, stop, enable, disable, and check status. You will learn the difference between an immediate action and a boot-time setting. Fourth, you will analyze service logs with journalctl and add time or follow filters to find relevant entries quickly. Each objective is paired with a short mnemonic or visual to help you remember when to inspect, when to signal, and when to consult logs. These are hands-on skills: you will use them during lab exercises to practice real-world scenarios such as starting a web server and reading its log output.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Focus
screens.narratorSegment: We will also frame these skills for hands-on practice. You will run commands to list processes, observe resource usage, and identify the PID of a target program. Then you will attempt a controlled termination, starting with a gentle request for shutdown and then a forced stop only if the process ignores the request. For services, you will practice starting a web service, checking its status, enabling it to start at boot, and finally disabling and stopping it. Reading logs will be part of every exercise: you will follow recent log entries to verify that your changes produced the expected behavior. Each objective will have a simple mnemonic to help you remember this flow: Observe → Request → Verify → Persist. This pattern reduces mistakes such as using a hard kill too early or forgetting to enable critical services for reboot persistence.

screens.title: Processes vs Services
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define processes and services and clarify how they differ in behavior and management. A process is any running instance of a program and has a unique process identifier, or PID. It may be started interactively by a user, spawned by another program, or created at boot by an init system. A service, sometimes called a daemon, is a specialized background process that provides system functionality and is managed by systemd on RHEL. Services are described by unit files that tell systemd how and when to start them. The distinction matters operationally: a transient process might be killed without system integration, but a service is controlled through systemctl and typically has defined startup and shutdown semantics. Example: running a script in your shell creates a process with a PID; installing and enabling httpd creates a service so the web server will be managed and restarted by systemd as configured. A common misconception is to treat services like ordinary processes and try to stop them only with kill; this can leave systemd thinking the service is active or cause automated restarts. Always prefer systemctl for services so that their unit state and logs remain consistent. As a takeaway, think: use process tools to inspect and diagnose, and use systemctl to control service lifecycle and persistence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Processes vs Services
Definition

Process

An instance of a running program with a unique PID and runtime resource usage. Can be transient or long-lived.

Example
You run a maintenance script from your shell. It appears as a process with a PID and exits when finished.
Common misconception
Killing a service process directly may leave systemd confused or cause an automatic restart. Prefer systemctl for managed services.
Definition

Service (Daemon)

A background process managed by systemd via unit files that can be started, stopped, and configured to run at boot.

Example
Installing and enabling the httpd package creates a service so the web server can be started at boot and managed centrally.
Key Takeaway

Inspect processes with ps/top, but control services through systemctl to keep unit state and logs coherent.

screens.title: Listing and Inspecting Processes with ps
screens.narratorSegment: The ps command is your first line of investigation when you need a snapshot of running processes. A commonly used form is ps aux, which shows all processes, including those of other users and those not attached to a terminal. Important columns to read are USER, PID, %C P U, %MEM and the COMMAND. USER tells you who started the process, PID is the unique identifier used by other tools, %C P U and %MEM help you spot resource hogs, and COMMAND shows the program and arguments. A concrete example: running ps aux | grep httpd helps you find the PIDs of Apache worker processes so you can examine or signal them. A frequent learner mistake is to assume ps reports live changing values — ps is a snapshot. For ongoing monitoring use top or htop. Another misconception is trusting a process name alone; several programs can share the same command name, so verify with PID and user. As a quick workflow: run ps aux, filter with grep for a target name, confirm the PID and user, then decide whether to send a signal or consult service management for a unit that owns that process. Practice this until reading these columns is second nature.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › ps aux
Command
ps aux
ps aux | grep httpd
Read these columns
  • USER: who owns the process
  • PID: unique process identifier used by kill and other tools
  • %CPU / %MEM: quick way to find resource hogs
  • COMMAND: program name and arguments
Example
To find Apache worker PIDs: ps aux | grep httpd. Confirm the PID and user before signaling.
Common mistake
Relying on process name alone can misidentify a process. Always pair name with PID and USER when taking action.
Key Takeaway

ps aux is a snapshot that helps you find PIDs and resource usage before taking any action.

screens.title: top and htop for Real-Time Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: top and htop provide dynamic, updating views of processes so you can monitor C P U and memory usage as they change. top is available by default and shows a sorted list of processes with a system summary including total tasks, C P U load, and memory usage. It allows quick keyboard-driven sorting and easy identification of the highest consumers. htop, when installed, enhances the experience with color-coding, a tree view, and mouse support, making navigation and process manipulation easier. For instance, htop makes it straightforward to select a process and send a signal from the interface. A concrete example: run top to spot a process steadily eating C P U over minutes; then run htop to visually inspect child processes and memory distribution. A common mistake is to rely solely on one refresh and not watch trends — spikes and sustained high usage are different problems. Also, remember that htop may not be installed by default; install it using the package manager when you need its features. Use top when you need immediate availability and htop when you want richer interaction and visual grouping of processes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › top vs htop
top (default)
top
# Shows CPU, tasks, and a dynamic list sorted by CPU by default

Available on a default install, useful for quick investigation and low-overhead monitoring.

htop (optional)
sudo dnf install htop -y
htop
# Color, tree view, mouse and easier signaling

When you need better interaction and a clearer visual grouping of processes, htop is helpful. Install when appropriate.

When to use

Use top for immediate checks and htop when you need color, tree view, or interactive signaling to inspect relationships between processes.

Misconception

Seeing a high CPU value once doesn't prove a leak; observe behavior over time before killing processes.

screens.title: Signals and kill: Safe Termination Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: When a process misbehaves, signals allow you to request that it change state or exit. The default polite signal is SIGTERM, which asks a process to terminate cleanly and lets it close files and release resources. Send it using kill PID. If a process ignores SIGTERM, you can escalate to SIGKILL with kill -9 PID, which forcibly and immediately terminates the process without cleanup. Because SIGKILL can cause data corruption if the process was writing files, reserve it as a last resort. killall process_name terminates all processes with a matching name and is dangerous when multiple instances are legitimate. A practical example: if data_processor is stuck, first run ps aux to confirm PID, then kill PID to send SIGTERM. If it remains, check logs and then use kill -9 only if stopping the process immediately is essential to protect system stability. A common mistake is issuing SIGKILL reflexively; that can leave open files and inconsistent state. Always verify the PID and check whether a process is managed by systemd; if so, prefer systemctl stop to allow unit-level handling and logging. Your decision tree should favor graceful shutdown, verification, and escalation only when necessary.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Signals & kill
Common signals
kill PID          # sends SIGTERM (15) by default
kill -9 PID       # sends SIGKILL (9)
killall name       # kills all processes with that name
SIGTERM requests a clean shutdown. SIGKILL forces immediate termination and should be used with care.
Cautionary example
If a database writer gets killed with SIGKILL while writing, you can leave files in an inconsistent state. Prefer graceful signals and check application logs first.
Check your understanding

Before using kill -9, confirm PID, try SIGTERM, and consult service management if the process is part of a unit.

screens.title: systemd and systemctl Basics
screens.narratorSegment: systemd is the init system on RHEL that manages units such as services. The primary tool for interacting with systemd is systemctl. Use systemctl status service_name to view the service state and recent journal entries; it reports whether a service is active, inactive, or failed and shows short logs for quick diagnostics. To change runtime state, use sudo systemctl start or sudo systemctl stop. Restart stops and then starts the service, while reload tells a service to re-read its configuration if it supports a reload operation, which is less disruptive than a restart. For example, if you change a web server's configuration and the server supports reload, prefer sudo systemctl reload httpd so existing connections are preserved when possible. A common misunderstanding is confusing reload with enable; reload changes runtime configuration, enable affects boot-time behavior. Always check systemctl status after an operation to confirm the desired state and see hints in the output. Remember that systemctl is the correct interface for service lifecycle management; directly killing a process that belongs to a unit may lead systemd to attempt a restart depending on the unit settings.

keyIdea.title: systemctl actions
keyIdea.text: Use start/stop/restart/reload for runtime control and status to verify; prefer reload for non-disruptive configuration changes when supported.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › systemctl basics
Common commands
systemctl status httpd
sudo systemctl start httpd
sudo systemctl stop httpd
sudo systemctl restart httpd
sudo systemctl reload httpd
Use status to confirm state and read short logs. Prefer reload for configuration changes when the service supports it; restart is more disruptive but guarantees a clean start.
Practical hint
After starting or changing a service, run systemctl status to verify and inspect recent log lines embedded in the status output.
Misconception

enable does not start a service now; it only makes the service start at boot.

screens.title: Enable and Disable: Controlling Boot Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding enable and disable is critical to controlling service behavior across reboots. systemctl enable creates the necessary links so that systemd will start a service automatically during boot. systemctl disable removes those links so the service will not auto-start after a reboot. Importantly, enable and disable do not change the current runtime state — enabling a service does not start it immediately and disabling does not stop a running instance. For example, you might start a service to test it with sudo systemctl start httpd, then run sudo systemctl enable httpd to make sure it starts after the next reboot. A common mistake is to enable a service and assume it has been started; always verify with status. Another pitfall is forgetting to enable critical services before maintenance, which can lead to services not coming back online after a reboot. The safe workflow is to start or stop a service to affect runtime behavior, and separately enable or disable to affect persistence across boots. This separation lets you test changes without altering boot configuration until you're ready. Enable and Disable: Controlling Boot Behavior means enable/disable modify boot-time startup links, while start/stop affect the running system immediately. verify with status after each change.. In practical terms, what enable/disable does and why it’s separate from start/stop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Enable vs Start
Enable / Disable
sudo systemctl enable httpd
sudo systemctl disable httpd

These commands change whether systemd will start the service automatically during boot, but do not immediately start or stop the service.

Start / Stop
sudo systemctl start httpd
sudo systemctl stop httpd

These commands change the service state immediately for the running system but do not alter boot-time behavior.

Key Takeaway

Manage runtime and boot persistence separately: start/stop now, enable/disable for the future.

screens.title: Reading Service Logs with journalctl
screens.narratorSegment: journalctl is the central tool for viewing logs captured by systemd's journal. To see logs for a particular service, use journalctl -u service_name; this shows entries only for that unit. For example, journalctl -u httpd displays the web server's messages so you can see startup errors or warnings. Use journalctl -u httpd -f to follow new log lines in real time while reproducing an issue. If you only need recent entries, add --since "2 hours ago" or another time window to narrow results. A practical workflow for troubleshooting: start by checking systemctl status to see the unit state and short logs, then run journalctl -u to inspect full history, and finally follow with -f while you replicate the issue. A common mistake is searching system-wide logs for clues before narrowing to the service unit; filtering by unit makes diagnosis quicker. Another misconception is assuming journalctl duplicates /var/log files; systemd-journald centralizes logs and provides richer filtering. The goal is to combine status, unit logs, and live following to pinpoint configuration or runtime errors efficiently. Reading Service Logs with journalctl means filter logs by unit with -u, follow with -f, and use --since or --until to bound time ranges for focused troubleshooting.. In practical terms, how to target unit logs, follow output, and restrict by time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › journalctl
Inspect unit logs
journalctl -u httpd
journalctl -u httpd -f
journalctl -u httpd --since "2 hours ago"

Start with systemctl status for a quick view, then drill into journalctl for full context and follow new entries while testing.

Practical example
After starting httpd, use journalctl -u httpd --since "5 minutes ago" to verify that no startup errors occurred and that listeners bound successfully.
Key Takeaway

Use unit-scoped logs and time filters to rapidly find relevant entries for a service without noise from unrelated system messages.

screens.title: Practice: Install and Manage a Web Service
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through managing a simple web service so you can practice the Observe → Request → Verify → Persist pattern. First, install the web server package using the package manager. An example command is sudo dnf install httpd -y. After installation, check its initial status with systemctl status httpd; you will likely see it inactive and disabled on a fresh install. Next, start the service with sudo systemctl start httpd and verify that it is active. To ensure it starts after reboot, enable it with sudo systemctl enable httpd. Now inspect the running processes with ps aux | grep httpd to note worker PIDs. If you need to view logs, run journalctl -u httpd --since "5 minutes ago" or follow live logs with -f. To stop and clean up, use sudo systemctl stop httpd and sudo systemctl disable httpd, then confirm status. A common mistake is enabling without starting and then assuming the service is running; always confirm with status and logs. This exercise ties together package installation, service lifecycle commands, process inspection, and log verification in a single, repeatable workflow.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Practice: httpd
Lab steps
  1. Install: sudo dnf install httpd -y
  2. Check status: systemctl status httpd
  3. Start: sudo systemctl start httpd
  4. Enable at boot: sudo systemctl enable httpd
  5. Inspect processes: ps aux | grep httpd
  6. View logs: journalctl -u httpd --since "5 minutes ago"
  7. Stop and disable when done: sudo systemctl stop httpd && sudo systemctl disable httpd
Example verification
systemctl status httpd
# look for: Active: active (running)
journalctl -u httpd -f
# follow live logs while requesting a reload or testing a request
Key Takeaway

Practice the sequence until confirming status and logs are second nature: install, start, enable, inspect, verify, stop, disable.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Patterns and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting a service or process requires a calm, methodical approach. Begin by gathering facts: check systemctl status for the unit, list processes with ps aux to see PIDs and users, and inspect recent logs with journalctl -u to find error messages. If a process is consuming resources, watch with top or htop to determine if the usage is transient or sustained. Before sending signals, ask whether the process belongs to a systemd unit; if it does, prefer systemctl stop or restart so systemd can run the unit's shutdown and any configured recovery. Avoid kill -9 unless the process is unresponsive and you accept the potential for data loss. Common errors include enabling a service but not starting it, killing related processes without checking for children, and failing to check logs for configuration errors after a restart. A practical checklist: observe, attempt a graceful action, verify status and logs, and only then escalate to forceful termination. This reduces surprises and helps you preserve service integrity while resolving issues. Troubleshooting Patterns and Pitfalls means observe status and logs, try graceful actions, verify effects, and only escalate to forceful kills if necessary while understanding the risk.. In practical terms, checks to run before escalating and how to avoid common errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Troubleshooting Patterns
Checklist
  • Run systemctl status for the service and read embedded journal lines.
  • List processes with ps aux and confirm PID and owner before signaling.
  • Watch resource trends with top or htop to distinguish spikes from leaks.
  • Use journalctl -u <unit> --since or -f when reproducing issues.
  • If the unit manages the process, prefer systemctl stop/restart over kill.
Avoid
Reaching immediately for kill -9 or killall without checking service ownership and logs first.
Do
Follow Observe → Request → Verify → Persist and confirm effects with status and journal entries.

screens.title: Quick Assessment: Choose the Right Command
screens.narratorSegment: Let's practice decision-making with two short scenarios so you build instinct around the right command. Scenario one: a configuration change requires the service to re-read settings without dropping connections. The correct action is to request a reload with systemctl reload service_name if the service supports it. This is less disruptive than restart. Scenario two: a single background job started from a shell is consuming 100% C P U and the system is unresponsive. Here, you might use kill -9 PID as an emergency step, but only after trying kill PID and confirming that it is not a managed unit. When answering these questions, always justify the choice: did you check unit ownership, logs, or child processes? A common error is to treat all problems as service issues and use systemctl when the offending process is not part of a unit, or conversely to use kill when systemctl would preserve unit metadata and logs. After each scenario, ask yourself: Did I observe? Did I try a graceful approach? Will this action affect boot behavior? These quick checks build safer habits. Quick Assessment: Choose the Right Command means choose reload for config changes, prefer graceful signals, and reserve kill -9 for emergencies after verifying process ownership and logs.. In practical terms, practice questions to test judgment between process and service actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Assessment
Scenario 1
You updated a web server configuration and want minimal disruption. Choose between reload and restart.
Best choice: systemctl reload service_name if supported; it re-reads config without a full stop. Restart is more disruptive.
Scenario 2
A background process started from shell consumes 95% CPU and ignores SIGTERM. The system is sluggish.
Best choice: try kill PID, verify; if unresponsive and critical, use kill -9 PID. Confirm it is not a managed unit before using systemctl.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's capture the essential concepts to carry forward. First, a process is a running instance of a program with a PID; use ps, top, and htop to inspect and monitor processes. Second, a service is a managed background process under systemd and should be controlled with systemctl so unit state, logging, and boot behavior remain consistent. Third, signals are how you communicate with processes: start with SIGTERM and escalate to SIGKILL only when necessary, and avoid aggressive use of killall. Fourth, systemctl offers start, stop, restart and reload for runtime control, and enable and disable to configure boot-time behavior. Fifth, journalctl centralizes logs and should be your first stop for unit-specific troubleshooting. Finally, follow the Observe → Request → Verify → Persist pattern: inspect before acting, prefer graceful actions, verify with status and logs, and alter boot behavior only when ready. These key ideas form the backbone of safe, repeatable system administration practices on RHEL.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we will build a clear mental model of processes and services on RHEL and learn the essential commands you will use every day. A process is a running instance of a program, and a service is a background process that systemd manages continuously. You will see how to inspect active programs with tools like ps, top, and htop; how to send signals to stop misbehaving processes with kill; and how to control systemd services with systemctl start, stop, restart, reload, enable and disable. We will also cover how to read service logs with journalctl for effective troubleshooting. These skills matter because they let you keep services available, diagnose resource issues, and avoid data loss by choosing the right action. For example, you will learn when to request a graceful shutdown versus when a forced kill is appropriate. By the end of this lesson you will be able to list processes, identify PIDs, safely stop a runaway program, and manage service startup behavior so your system boots into the correct state. As you watch, think about which commands you would use to investigate a slow server and which to use only as a last resort.

In this chapter we focus on four practical skills that form the foundation of process and service management on RHEL. First, you will learn to identify and understand system processes using viewing tools. This means reading columns like PID, USER, C P U and memory and recognizing what a runaway process looks like. Second, you will practice controlling processes by sending signals with safe defaults first, then escalations only when necessary. That skill keeps systems stable without risking corruption. Third, you will manage services using systemd through the systemctl commands to start, stop, enable, disable, and check status. You will learn the difference between an immediate action and a boot-time setting. Fourth, you will analyze service logs with journalctl and add time or follow filters to find relevant entries quickly. Each objective is paired with a short mnemonic or visual to help you remember when to inspect, when to signal, and when to consult logs. These are hands-on skills: you will use them during lab exercises to practice real-world scenarios such as starting a web server and reading its log output.

We will also frame these skills for hands-on practice. You will run commands to list processes, observe resource usage, and identify the PID of a target program. Then you will attempt a controlled termination, starting with a gentle request for shutdown and then a forced stop only if the process ignores the request. For services, you will practice starting a web service, checking its status, enabling it to start at boot, and finally disabling and stopping it. Reading logs will be part of every exercise: you will follow recent log entries to verify that your changes produced the expected behavior. That sequencing matters — inspect first, take a safe action, verify with status and logs, and only escalate if necessary. Each objective will have a simple mnemonic to help you remember this flow: Observe → Request → Verify → Persist. This pattern reduces mistakes such as using a hard kill too early or forgetting to enable critical services for reboot persistence.

Let's define processes and services and clarify how they differ in behavior and management. A process is any running instance of a program and has a unique process identifier, or PID. It may be started interactively by a user, spawned by another program, or created at boot by an init system. A service, sometimes called a daemon, is a specialized background process that provides system functionality and is managed by systemd on RHEL. Services are described by unit files that tell systemd how and when to start them. The distinction matters operationally: a transient process might be killed without system integration, but a service is controlled through systemctl and typically has defined startup and shutdown semantics. Example: running a script in your shell creates a process with a PID; installing and enabling httpd creates a service so the web server will be managed and restarted by systemd as configured. A common misconception is to treat services like ordinary processes and try to stop them only with kill; this can leave systemd thinking the service is active or cause automated restarts. Always prefer systemctl for services so that their unit state and logs remain consistent. As a takeaway, think: use process tools to inspect and diagnose, and use systemctl to control service lifecycle and persistence.

The ps command is your first line of investigation when you need a snapshot of running processes. A commonly used form is ps aux, which shows all processes, including those of other users and those not attached to a terminal. Important columns to read are USER, PID, %C P U, %MEM and the COMMAND. USER tells you who started the process, PID is the unique identifier used by other tools, %C P U and %MEM help you spot resource hogs, and COMMAND shows the program and arguments. A concrete example: running ps aux | grep httpd helps you find the PIDs of Apache worker processes so you can examine or signal them. A frequent learner mistake is to assume ps reports live changing values — ps is a snapshot. For ongoing monitoring use top or htop. Another misconception is trusting a process name alone; several programs can share the same command name, so verify with PID and user. As a quick workflow: run ps aux, filter with grep for a target name, confirm the PID and user, then decide whether to send a signal or consult service management for a unit that owns that process. Practice this until reading these columns is second nature.

top and htop provide dynamic, updating views of processes so you can monitor C P U and memory usage as they change. top is available by default and shows a sorted list of processes with a system summary including total tasks, C P U load, and memory usage. It allows quick keyboard-driven sorting and easy identification of the highest consumers. htop, when installed, enhances the experience with color-coding, a tree view, and mouse support, making navigation and process manipulation easier. For instance, htop makes it straightforward to select a process and send a signal from the interface. A concrete example: run top to spot a process steadily eating C P U over minutes; then run htop to visually inspect child processes and memory distribution. A common mistake is to rely solely on one refresh and not watch trends — spikes and sustained high usage are different problems. Also, remember that htop may not be installed by default; install it using the package manager when you need its features. Use top when you need immediate availability and htop when you want richer interaction and visual grouping of processes.

When a process misbehaves, signals allow you to request that it change state or exit. The default polite signal is SIGTERM, which asks a process to terminate cleanly and lets it close files and release resources. Send it using kill PID. If a process ignores SIGTERM, you can escalate to SIGKILL with kill -9 PID, which forcibly and immediately terminates the process without cleanup. Because SIGKILL can cause data corruption if the process was writing files, reserve it as a last resort. killall process_name terminates all processes with a matching name and is dangerous when multiple instances are legitimate. A practical example: if data_processor is stuck, first run ps aux to confirm PID, then kill PID to send SIGTERM. If it remains, check logs and then use kill -9 only if stopping the process immediately is essential to protect system stability. A common mistake is issuing SIGKILL reflexively; that can leave open files and inconsistent state. Always verify the PID and check whether a process is managed by systemd; if so, prefer systemctl stop to allow unit-level handling and logging. Your decision tree should favor graceful shutdown, verification, and escalation only when necessary.

systemd is the init system on RHEL that manages units such as services. The primary tool for interacting with systemd is systemctl. Use systemctl status service_name to view the service state and recent journal entries; it reports whether a service is active, inactive, or failed and shows short logs for quick diagnostics. To change runtime state, use sudo systemctl start or sudo systemctl stop. Restart stops and then starts the service, while reload tells a service to re-read its configuration if it supports a reload operation, which is less disruptive than a restart. For example, if you change a web server's configuration and the server supports reload, prefer sudo systemctl reload httpd so existing connections are preserved when possible. A common misunderstanding is confusing reload with enable; reload changes runtime configuration, enable affects boot-time behavior. Always check systemctl status after an operation to confirm the desired state and see hints in the output. Remember that systemctl is the correct interface for service lifecycle management; directly killing a process that belongs to a unit may lead systemd to attempt a restart depending on the unit settings.

Understanding enable and disable is critical to controlling service behavior across reboots. systemctl enable creates the necessary links so that systemd will start a service automatically during boot. systemctl disable removes those links so the service will not auto-start after a reboot. Importantly, enable and disable do not change the current runtime state — enabling a service does not start it immediately and disabling does not stop a running instance. For example, you might start a service to test it with sudo systemctl start httpd, then run sudo systemctl enable httpd to make sure it starts after the next reboot. A common mistake is to enable a service and assume it has been started; always verify with status. Another pitfall is forgetting to enable critical services before maintenance, which can lead to services not coming back online after a reboot. The safe workflow is to start or stop a service to affect runtime behavior, and separately enable or disable to affect persistence across boots. This separation lets you test changes without altering boot configuration until you're ready. For example, journalctl -u httpd displays the web server's messages so you can see startup errors or warnings. Another misconception is assuming journalctl duplicates /var/log files; systemd-journald centralizes logs and provides richer filtering.
